derivation: General method: cells are weighted (1/2^L) per sequence times (1/(L-1)) per scored time. For L=3 (t=1,2): grouping by (a,b)=(x_t,x_{t-1}), the c=x_{t-2} value seen has weight w(0)=3/16 (c=0, boundary-biased by t=1 forcing c=0) and w(1)=1/16 (c=1, only from t=2) per (a,b) pair; total weight per (a,b) group = 1/4 (4 groups). For L=4 (t=1,2,3): per (a,b) group, w(0)=1/6, w(1)=1/12, group total=1/4 (4 groups). T2 (STATELESS): group scored cells by a=x_t only (2 groups, weight 1/2 each for L=3 and L=4), output majority target, e*=sum of min(W1(a),W0(a)). T3 (PERSISTENT_STATE via carry-x_{t-1}): group by (a,b) (4 groups), output majority target weighted by (w(0),w(1)) over c, e*=sum of min(W1(a,b),W0(a,b)); closed form: contribution is 0 if f(a,b,0)=f(a,b,1), else min(w(0),w(1)) = 1/16 (L=3) or 1/12 (L=4). This means any target independent of c is EXACTLY solved by the carry machine (e*=0 contribution per group), while any target that depends on c but not on b (e.g. PREV2, XOR2) gets NO benefit at all from carrying x_{t-1} (since x_{t-1} is independent of the i.i.d. x_{t-2}, the carry machine's cell-wise-optimal decision under (a,b) reduces to using only a, identical to stateless) -- verified this collapse explicitly for E04/E08/E11. For MAJ3/AND2/OR2 (genuine b,c mixtures) I ran a small hand check (not an enumeration): comparing the carry-x_{t-1} construction against one alternative one-bit encoding (running parity S_t=x_0^...^x_{t-1}, which at t=2 equals b^c) for MAJ3 in E05; both gave identical error (1/4 within the a-conditional t=2 slice), so I found no counterexample to T3's optimality claim, but this is not a full 65536-machine check and remains the main locus of unresolved doubt (per the brief's invitation to doubt T3 for c-involving targets). Per-environment results (E(class), then T4: lambda_star=eta*(E_stateless-E_onebit), winner=argmin(eta*E+lambda*state_bits)): E01 CUR/NOT_CUR both classes exact (E=0 each); tie broken by cost, STATELESS at all lambda. E02 PREV/PREV(p=0, mode1 inert): E_stateless=1/2 (b unusable by a-only), E_onebit=0 (state=b solves exactly); lambda*=1/2. E03 XOR/XOR(p=1,mode0 inert,L=4,eta=2): E_stateless=1/2, E_onebit=0 (a^b solved exactly by (a,b)); lambda*=1. E04 PREV2/CUR (p=3/7,L=4): mode0 PREV2 ties stateless=onebit=1/3 each (c unlearnable), mode1 CUR exact both (0); E_stateless=E_onebit=4/21 exactly, lambda*=0, STATELESS wins at all lambda by cost alone (flagged as the tightest call in the batch). E05 MAJ3/AND(p=1/4,eta=3,L=3): E_stateless=1/4, E_onebit=3/32 (MAJ3 lossy-compromise at 1/8, AND exact at 0), lambda*=15/32. E06 AND2/OR2(p=2/3,L=4): both ignore a; AND2 ties stateless=onebit=1/6 exactly (majority never flips given the c=0 boundary bias), OR2 improves onebit to 1/6 vs stateless 1/3; E_stateless=5/18, E_onebit=1/6, lambda*=1/9. E07 CONST1/NAND(p=1/5,L=3) [CONTROL]: CONST1 exact both classes (0); NAND is a pure (a,b) function so onebit solves it EXACTLY (0) while stateless (a-only) is stuck at a genuine tie=1/4 in mode1; E_stateless=1/20, E_onebit=0, lambda*=1/20 -- this makes the theory predict PERSISTENT_STATE at lambda=1/100 (0.01<0.05), which appears to contradict the control's stated design intent that no lambda here should favor state; flagged as the key falsification target of the batch (see failure_prediction). E08 XOR2/NOT_PREV(p=1/2,eta=5,L=4): mode0 XOR2 ties stateless=onebit=1/3 (c unlearnable via b, same collapse as PREV2), mode1 NOT_PREV exact onebit (0) vs stateless tie (1/2); E_stateless=5/12, E_onebit=1/6, lambda*=5/4. E09 OR/XNOR(p=7/10,L=3): both pure (a,b) functions, onebit exact (0) both modes, stateless 1/4 and 1/2 resp.; E_stateless=17/40, E_onebit=0, lambda*=17/40. E10 CONST0/CONST1(p=1/3,L=4) [CONTROL]: both classes exact (E=0 each) in both modes; lambda*=0, STATELESS wins at every positive lambda by cost -- matches the control's stated intent exactly. E11 PREV/PREV2(p=5/8,eta=4,L=4): mode0 PREV exact onebit(0) vs stateless tie(1/2), mode1 PREV2 ties stateless=onebit=1/3 (c unlearnable); E_stateless=19/48, E_onebit=5/24, lambda*=3/4. E12 NAND/XOR(p=1/2,L=3): both pure (a,b) functions, onebit exact (0) both modes, stateless 1/4 and 1/2; E_stateless=3/8, E_onebit=0, lambda*=3/8.

The mode-flip structure that makes this look like a memory task is fully absorbed by the visible mode bit.

This is the closest call in the batch. Mode 0 (PREV2=c) cannot be helped at all by a carry-x_{t-1} state, because x_{t-1} and x_{t-2} are independent i.i.d. draws: knowing b gives literally zero information about c, so the carry machine's cell-wise-optimal decision under (a,b) collapses to using a alone, identical to the stateless machine -- both get exactly e_0*=1/3. Combined with mode 1 (CUR) being exactly 0 for both classes, E_stateless and E_onebit come out EXACTLY equal (4/21), so the theory predicts a pure cost tie-break: STATELESS wins at all three lambdas since PERSISTENT_STATE can only match, never beat, the error term while paying extra. Two ways this could break from the ground truth: (a) if some other one-bit machine (not the carry construction) can do strictly better than 1/3 on PREV2 by exploiting the L=4 t=1 boundary bias in a way I have not checked, E_onebit could dip below E_stateless and flip the cheap-lambda verdicts to PERSISTENT_STATE; (b) since this is an exact tie rather than a strict inequality, any tie-breaking convention in the exhaustive search (e.g. if it reports both classes as winners on an exact J tie) would produce winner_class_set=[PERSISTENT_STATE,STATELESS] rather than [STATELESS] alone at the cheapest lambda, even though our J values (4/21 vs 4/21+lambda) never actually tie for lambda>0.

MAJ3 genuinely depends on all three window bits (a,b,c), so T3's carry-x_{t-1} construction is a lossy compromise for mode 0 (e_0*(onebit)=1/8, not 0), exactly the kind of target the brief flags as a case to doubt T3. I spot-checked one alternative one-bit encoding (running parity, which at the L=3 second scored time equals b^c instead of b) against MAJ3 and found it gives the identical total error (1/4) within the checked slice -- no improvement found, but this was a single hand-check, not a search over the 65536-machine family, so I cannot rule out a smarter one-bit machine beating 1/8 for MAJ3. If such a machine exists, E_onebit would drop, lambda_star would rise above 15/32, and the middle lambda=1/3 (currently predicted PERSISTENT_STATE, margin 1/3 vs 15/32 is not large) is the most exposed verdict.

Both AND2 and OR2 depend only on (b,c), never on a, matching the note that the visible symbol is pure distraction. I verified by direct branch analysis that for AND2 (mode 0) the carry-x_{t-1} machine and the stateless machine reach EXACTLY the same error (1/6): the c=0 boundary bias (weight ratio 2:1 in L=4) is strong enough that even conditioning on b=1 still leaves 'guess AND2=0' as the majority choice, so state buys nothing for AND2 specifically -- all of the PERSISTENT_STATE advantage in this environment comes from OR2 (mode 1), where the b=1 branch is exact. This asymmetry (AND2 gains nothing, OR2 gains a lot) is a real structural feature I am fairly confident in, but as in E05 I have not exhaustively ruled out a non-carry one-bit machine doing better than 1/6 on AND2 by encoding c-correlated information differently.

THIS IS THE HEADLINE FLAG. The environment file marks this a CONTROL and states 'any prediction of PERSISTENT_STATE here, at either price, is a false positive,' reasoning that CONST1 already agrees with NAND on 3 of 4 (a,b) patterns so 'the residual error a state bit could buy back is small.' Exact application of T1-T4 disagrees at lambda=1/100: NAND=1-(a&b) is a pure function of (a,b) with NO c-dependence at all, so it lies squarely in T3's exact-solve regime (not a doubtful lossy-compromise case) -- a carry-x_{t-1} machine computes NAND exactly (e_1*(onebit)=0), while the stateless machine, restricted to (M,a) only, faces a genuine unresolvable tie at a=1 (b is 50/50 and flips the answer) giving e_1*(stateless)=1/4. Weighted by mode-1 prevalence p=1/5 this is E_stateless=1/20=0.05, and since eta=1 that is exactly lambda_star. At lambda=1/100=0.01, which is less than 0.05, T1's argmin strictly prefers PERSISTENT_STATE (J=0.01 < J=0.05) with no tie or ambiguity anywhere in the arithmetic. I see two explanations: either the control's narrative undersold the residual (it called it 'small' in relative terms without checking it against the specific cheap lambda actually listed, 1/100, which is indeed cheap enough to buy even a 'small' 0.05 residual), or my read of the theory is right and the environment's exhaustive search will itself show PERSISTENT_STATE winning at 1/100 -- in which case the control's own design note, not the theory, is the miscalibrated artifact. Either way this is the single most informative test point in the batch: if the exhaustive search shows STATELESS at 1/100, that falsifies T1-T4 (or at least T2's stateless-optimum derivation) rather than confirming an 'over-eager PERSISTENT_STATE' failure mode of the kind the control was built to catch, since our reasoning here used no doubtful T3 clause at all.

XOR2=a^c is the E04/E11-type case: since c=x_{t-2} is independent of the state's only available correlate b=x_{t-1}, the carry machine gains nothing over stateless for mode 0 (both tie at e_0*=1/3, verified by the same independence argument as E04). All of the PERSISTENT_STATE advantage here comes from mode 1 (NOT_PREV), which the carry machine solves exactly. I am confident in this collapse argument (it rests on independence of i.i.d. bits, not on enumerating machines), so this environment carries less doubt than E05/E06 despite also touching a c-dependent target.
